Six countries on this map of Europe in June 1941 were officially neutral.

Not one of them was actually uninvolved.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Sweden, dark blue and untouched. It supplied Germany with iron ore through the war and, weeks after this map, allowed a fully armed German division to cross Swedish territory by rail from Norway to Finland. Stockholm called it a transit permit.

2/ Switzerland, small and surrounded. It kept its army mobilised and its passes mined, and it also cleared German gold, much of it looted, through its banks. Neutrality here was a business model as well as a defensive posture.

3/ Spain, yellow. Franco met Hitler at Hendaye in October 1940, listened to the terms for joining, and declined. Then, once Germany invaded the USSR, he sent tens of thousands of Spanish volunteers east as the Blue Division. Non-belligerent, not neutral.

4/ Portugal, green. Bound to Britain by an alliance dating to 1373 — the oldest still in force — while selling tungsten to both sides at wartime prices. In 1943 it leased bases in the Azores to the Allies without leaving neutrality.

5/ Ireland, light green. It stayed formally neutral against considerable British pressure, but quietly returned Allied airmen who landed there while interning German ones, and shared weather reports that mattered for D-Day.

6/ Turkey, dark red. On 18 June 1941 — four days before Barbarossa — it signed a treaty of friendship with Germany. It also sold chromite to both sides and declared war on Germany only in February 1945, when it was safe and useful.

7/ And the largest neutral of all isn't marked as one. The Soviet Union was Germany's trading partner in June 1941, shipping grain, oil and manganese west. Those trains were still running days before three million Axis troops crossed the border.

The full story of this map — the Axis at its widest, and why that was the problem — is in this week's Lines & Legends. Free, every 3 days: https://buttondown.com/forummapping
